Assassin's Creed Syndicate is considered to be the last old-school Assassin’s Creed title before the series shifted into the Action RPG genre. When released, it also flew under the radar after the messy launch of the previous title, Unity. People got burned and lost faith in the series after that, and Ubisoft had to take a break before the shift, so Syndicate is in a weird spot.
With all that aside, I found this game to be disappointingly average. I don’t know exactly what it is, but it’s simply not very interesting. The setting is nice, taking place in Victorian London. It has a steampunk vibe to it, taking place after the first industrial revolution. Some may not like that, but at least it’s something the series hasn't seen before.
You play as twins Jacob and Evie Frye, and outside the story, you can freely swap between them. Jacob is supposed to be a better brawler, and Evie better in stealth, but in practice, they play almost the same. The story is generic, mostly finding and executing the various Templar members in London until you eventually confront the leader.
They are disappointing, especially the leader since you have no connection with him, and he only appears in some cutscenes until the end. In most AC games, you have a more personal reason to deal with them, but this time it’s just a bad guy must die.
Gameplay is also average. Combat lacks the multi-kill sequences, and the cool kill animations are locked until enemies are put into a near-death state, which makes them much harder to trigger. You could argue that means combat is harder, but it’s just attack, counter, and break defense until you win. Enemies lack variety as well.
Parkouring feels a bit off. The first thing I noticed is that you have fewer opportunities for seamless parkour on rooftops because the streets are so wide compared to past games. The game gives you a grappling hook, which feels good to use, but at the same time feels like a band-aid to cover the mediocre parkouring.
Besides the story, you have the usual collectible hunting and side missions, which aren’t so bad. Historical figures are present as usual, this time featuring the likes of Charles Dickens, Charles Darwin, and Karl Marx.
However, collectibles have a HUGE catch. You can buy maps for most of them; however, two of them aren’t available in-game. Instead, they’re only available in the microtransactions store, with real money. A scummy tactic, since without those maps, you’ll need an external resource to find everything.
Stupid microtransactions, but at least besides these maps, there isn’t anything useful to buy. I bought the Gold Edition with the Season Pass, so I started with enough currency to buy one map, but I couldn’t naturally get enough to buy the other one. You can get more premium currency in-game, but it wasn’t enough for me to buy the other map. There is a way to farm slowly with temporary collectibles, but of course, most of the time, they are bugged and won’t count…
Speaking of the Season Pass, it doesn’t even give you all the content. Ten detective missions are available to buy, but it’s not included. They aren’t special but offer a different gameplay style you won’t find in the base game.
The main DLC content is the Jack the Ripper storyline, but it’s also disappointing. Very early on, you’re spoiled about its identity, and there’s only one new mechanic where you can fear your enemies. At least that feels satisfying to pull off.
The game also has a lot of small bugs, but nothing game-breaking I could find. The DLC, however, had one game-breaking bug that made me replay a side mission multiple times because a carriage would fly out of nowhere at the very end, killing an NPC and resulting in a fail. That was incredibly frustrating until after a few tries it worked fine.
The Ubisoft Connect also has its problems, mainly the lack of achievements and statistics in the in-game overlay. Let's start this recommendation with a bit of background information about my history with Assassin's Creed. It's important, yes, yes it is. 

I loved Assassin's Creed, ever since the first game, the one where you play as the weird monkey, I mean monk, Altair. You climb from building to building, start beating up people, stabbing them, jumping around, the bread and butter formula of Assassin's Creed. 

Assassin's Creed 2 took this system to a whole new level, with the introduction of Ezio, whom in my opinion, is still the best character in the entire series. Then came Brotherhood, Revelations, 3, Liberation, etc etc, it's all the same formula with slightly different changes per game. For instance, the Twin Blades in AC2, the Hookblade in Revelations, and the usage of recruits in Brotherhood.

The series, was awesome. 
HOWEVER, the Assassin's Creed did get plagued by several things, but mainly, Uplay, or as I'd like to call it, U-fking-play. It's horrible, AC2 was "DRM-ed" with having a constant connection to the servers, only problem being was that the servers happily cut off connection every 10 seconds, causing you to get booted from AC2. 

ANYWAY. After that massive screw over by Ubisoft with Unity, I decided to boycott the entire series. Microtransactions? Shitty performances even on my GTX970? Yeah, I was done with the AC series. Till Syndicate had a 40% sale, and I figured, hey let's give this game another chance! 

And I'm glad I did, for the first few hours anyway.

Let's talk about Graphics.
It's amazing, it's beautiful, and London is one huge city to explore. Most importantly, it runs on Ultra settings with my 970, something Unity failed to do even with 4x Titan Xs. Yeah, the optimization for this game is nicely done (after two weeks anyway).

Now moving on to Gameplay..
It's typical Assassin's Creed, you jump, you fly, you go left and right, you stab people. Except now, they make you choose between a stealth character or a brawling character. Some like the AC combat system, I personal prefer the stealth elements. Both characters share the same EXP pool, so you can switch between them as and when you like.

By the way, controls are dumb-ed down, you just hold one button to fly across the map. There's no elements such as  near fall, or any other more complicated buttons to press for that matter. It's literally a babi-ed Assassin's Creed, there's no more complexity that the older games delivered. 

How about the story?
It's, once again, a typical Assassin's Creed story. Assassin's trying to over throw Templars. It's been the same thing since the first game. AC1's Credits Song, AC2's Venice Rooftops, AC:B Master Assassin and even AC3's Main Theme, all of these had a lasting impact on the player because of the nature of the piece. At the time of writing this edit of my review, I have completed the game's campaign, a number of the character side missions, the Jack the Ripper DLC, and parts of The Last Maharajah and The Dreadful Crimes. 

I still recommend this entry in the franchise, but a more complete playthrough has somewhat lessened my esteem of it in some places. My largest complaint at this point would be the repetitiveness of the gameplay. Though there is variety in the objectives and action of the main story missions, they generally follow a consistent structure across the game - Jacob investigates the target, then assassinates them, while Evie cleans up the mess left in the wake of Jacob's last kill. Access to the last two of the game's nine sequences is locked behind liberation goals - to access sequence 8, you have to liberate 3 districts, and to access sequence 9, you have to have liberated the entire city. This means that to complete the story, you have to play every single liberation activity; kill every Templar, kidnap every gang leader, free every child labourer. It's exhausting. Here, there is no variety beyond variation in level design and optional objectives. 

The assassinations are still a highlight, carrying over the 'black box' sandboxes from Unity. Hunting a mad doctor in Lambeth Asylum; infiltrating an armoured carriage in Waterloo Station; stopping a robbery at the Bank of England; sneaking into Parliament; outmatching theatrics at the Alhambra. They are awesome. A large area within which to hunt your target, explore your options, create opportunities for yourself. And while the repeating structure of it does make it somewhat lose its appeal, it is interesting to see from Evie's perspective the consequences of each of these kills. It's always interesting when Assassin's Creed explores these angles instead of overly romanticising the Assassins as they did in AC2. It's simultaneously good lore-building while also adding depth to the portrayal of the group in Syndicate; Jacob's relentless pursuit of the London Templars gives rise to snake-oil medicine merchants, destabilises the transport sector, collapses the economy, and drives a stake through the heart of Whitehall. 

The characters are a standout as well. Jacob and Evie Fyre, our twin protagonists, present a somewhat engaging duality to the story, with Jacob being a brutish young man who's desperate to make a name for himself both in the Brotherhood and in the wider city, while Evie wants to stop the Templars in a more long-term way, preferring stealth to combat. This duality is sadly not extended to the gameplay, where they are identical with identical animations and movesets, having only 1-2 unique abilities each that are of little impact. 

The music by Austin Wintory is also a standout, something I have changed my tune on. It's lively, energetic, and perfect in tone for the setting. And it is so unlike anything that has come in Assassin's Creed before. 'A Gauntlet Scherzo', 'Bloody Presto con Brio' and 'The Assassin Two-Step' are highlights for me. The only complaint I have music-wise is that for some unfathomable reason, Ubisoft decided to leave 5 'murder ballads' written by Wintory out of the game. 'Give me the Cure', 'The Late Pearl Attaway', 'The Tale of Twopenny', 'Feasting on a Lord', and 'Jokes Jokes Jokes' all have lyrics lamenting the deaths of Jacob's 5 main targets, and they are absolutely brilliant, but they aren't in the game. 

1868 London is an interesting open world. Like all AC open worlds, it lacks the ways you can interact with it to make it feel more 'real', however, it is visually arresting and enjoyable to explore. As I mentioned in the original version of this review, the variety in the level design across the map, from the tight valleys of Whitechapel to the slums and factories of Southwark and the churning waters of the Thames, is interesting. The addition of driving allowing you to speed across the city is welcome. 

----------

I would strongly recommend Jack the Ripper and The Dreadful Crimes. The former takes the tone in a fittingly darker direction than the light humour of Quebec's Syndicate. There is still an element of repetition, as it asks you to do revised versions of the Liberation activities from the main game, but the story is much more focused and divorced from world progress, and tells a very interesting tale of Evie hunting the eponymous killer and asking 'what differentiates an Assassin from a serial killer?'. The addition of non-lethal fear attacks reinforces that philosophy, and though it took me a while to grasp it, it did a lot to enhance the more stealthy gameplay aspects. As for the Dreadful Crimes, they play very similarly to the murder mysteries in Unity, with a few improvements. You'll be introduced to a murder scene, and asked to figure out who did the killing. There's clues to examine, suspects to interrogate, and i found it actually tested my logic capabilities. A lot of fun.

[h1]Assassin's Creed Syndicate[/h1]
Syndicate is another Assassin's Creed game set in 19th century London.  I say another because not much has changed from the previous titles.  You get a third-person action-adventure RPG with the same basic fighting skills and controls as any other Assassin's Creed game.  What does Syndicate give you?  A step back on a new engine. 

[h1]What's Improved[/h1]
Syndicate is designed on the same engine as Unity and looks very much the same as Unity did last year only without the poorly opimized gameplay Unity had upon release (fixed four months later).  You get a new gadget to play with early on in the game, the grappling attachment to the assassin's blade.  Syndicate also takes a step back to older styled combat after fans complained that Unity was overly simplified which provides a steeper challenge, especially if you wander into an area a few levels higher.  

[h1]What's Unimproved[/h1]
I found navagating the city worse than Unity.  Unity for the most part was very decent except trying to jump off a fence or going into a window.  Syndicate's controls with a keyboard and mouse are worse. I can be climbing and trying to shimmy right with the "D" key pressed and Jacob shimmys left!  In just over 12 hours of gameplay, I have had this happen several times while trying to navigate support beams under bridges and the train stations. 

Another area I found disappointing was the lack of stats on gear choices that Unity introduced.  I rather enjoyed having so many options to load my character up with to attempt a stealth vs full on kill everything mission.  Syndicate takes another step back to the quest rewards and crafting gear with very limited options other than those found on outfits. 

[h1]Co-Op[/h1]
One aspect of Unity I really enjoyed was the Co-Op club activities I played with my 12 year old son.  We had a blast and as a result I have over two hundred hours in Unity which is double what I have in any other AC game and up to 5 times what I have in the older AC titles.  I was very disappointed that the Co-Op club activities were abandoned in Syndicate this time around as I found that to be one of the most redeeming qualities of Unity.  

[h1]The Story[/h1]
The story is good, not great.  It is the familar obtain the pieces of eden at any cost from or before the templars use them to destory the world with corrupt power. The best part of the sotry is that you get to play as two people.  The interaction between the twins (Jacob & Evie) really help to push the story along and make it fun. For the most part you can choose who you want to play with the exception of the story line which will force you to play one or the other at times.  

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
Graphically Syndicate looks as great as Unity did, maybe just a bit better.  The engine runs smooth although the system requirements are extremely steep.  Running triple SLI with 3x gtx 980s my frame rate will take a hit with everything on max settings but that may be in part due to a lack of sli support.  On a good note, the game still looks great on lower/mid cards such as a gtx 960 on low settings. Syndicate definitely looks better than Unity did on low settings. 

[h1]Pros[/h1]
Better combat
Better optimized graphics
Fun interaction between twin characters

[h1]Cons[/h1]
Controls are worse
No Co-Op club activities
Limited stats to build your character

[h1]Recommendation[/h1]
I was very disappointed in the absence of the Co-Op club activities, the poor control issues, and the lack of stats on gear for character custimization.  But in the end Syndicate does provide that very familar AC game experience if not over familar.  Syndicate is ejoyable although do not expect to spend several hundred hours in this title like you may have with AC IV Black Flag, AC Rogue, or AC Unity.  The content of ship battles, exploration, and Co-Op activities are just not there.

Fix for Assassin’s Creed Syndicate Crash on Startup

1. Launch the game.
2. As soon as the game starts booting, open Task Manager.
3. Look for ACS (it will likely be at the top since it uses a lot of memory).
4. Click “Go to details.”
5. Find ACS.exe.
6. Right-click it, select “Set priority”, then choose “Realtime.”
7. Close Task Manager and return to the game.

Notes
The game should run after this, but it may still be slightly buggy in some cases.

Part of this is due to a bit of personal bias - Victorian London has always been a favorite setting of mine and it's here in beautiful, meticulously detailed glory. But aside from that, the actual gameplay is improved, specifically with stealth and traversal. Botching a stealth kill doesn't automatically alert everyone and their mother within a 20 mile radius, and the zipline lets you avoid having to ponderously pick your way up every single building facade if you don't want to. Furthermore, each sidequest can be completed through a number of different methods, and there's not an overwhelming amount of stupid collectibles. And while the story itself is merely okay, the characters you meet and play as are all pretty charming and even legit funny. Syndcicate seems to be all about removing all the series' barriers between you and fun, and it's definitely working for me.

Assassin's Creed Syndicate is by far one of the most pleasing and visually appealing games of all time!
The game feels like a time machine that takes you to 19th-century London.
The map is huge, and it does feel more generation 9 than most current AAA titles out there to this date!
It captures the Industrial Revolution and the Victorian era properly, and it properly shows us the impact and suffering of London's citizens due to that.

I feel that the combat is weaker in most areas, and I genuinely believe that it lacks polish, especially when doing combos out there during Templar encounters.

The traversal is fun, as we now have a grapple gun to ascend from building to building and travel across all of London. Also yeah, we have good and smooth parkour implemented too.
Also, you can capture NPC carriages like we do in Watch Dogs and GTA games - a fun thing added there!

And yes, after all this, the main downside of the game is the storyline.
The story starts great, and everything keeps going great for the first few hours, but after the 3rd sequence, the storyline becomes flat.
And also, to be fair, the story feels rushed, as it seemed weird how they handled all the Templar Masterminds boss missions.
I mean, it was too much for the storyline, as most of those villains lacked motives and were technically slaves to their Templar Grand Master, Starrick Crawford; although he kinda portrays how leaders in the real world operate the world and their motives and all that.... you know!!!

You can choose either Assassin (Jacob Frye or Evie Frye) in most missions; however, it would be great if we got to see both the Frye twins together doing assassin stuff!
I really felt bad seeing their relationship lacking and getting distracted as the story progresses!
But anyways, Ubisoft should have hired a good writer for the storyline, but what's the point of mentioning it now after a decade!?!

Also the PC optimizations is bad, even worse than Assassin's Creed Unity, considering that this is a decade old game back from the PS4/Xbox One era (Gen 8) and on top of that it lacks a good Anti-Aliasing method.

Another bad thing is the microtransactions implemented into the game!

Overall, Assassin's Creed Syndicate is a great game when bought at a discounted price.
Also, please consider getting the 'Gold Edition' of the game to get all the story expansion content.

Syndicate betrays more traditional AC elements than it is loyal to. Jacob and Evie are already assassins when we meet them, so it’s not an origin story like Black Flag or Unity. Even so, their immaturity is reminiscent of those very games. 

The game allows you to play as both Jacob and Evie, to alternate between them outside and during some missions. I like that they aren’t just the same character gameplay wise, Jacob specialises in combat, while Evie in stealth, but Jacob is annoying. Unfortunately, for some reason, the game wants you to play as Jacob more and towards the end, most main missions are played as him. Evie deserves more screen time. The romance between Evie and Henry would have been acceptable if not for its lazy writing.

Syndicate’s Victorian London matches Unity’s Revolutionary Paris in attention to detail. However, unlike Paris, London’s tone is less on inequality between classes and more on how it was just a horrible place to live in in general. The city is monotonous enough that this message is successfully conveyed, yet has enough depth to make it interesting. The sky is polluted with smoke from factories in which children work and crime is rampant, yet through enough exploration, you’ll find people playing cricket, kids playing football, and couples taking photos. The game manages to draw a city so depressing and lifeless yet so immersive and full of life, and it looks incredible. Its size can be intimidating though, I found myself fast travelling a lot compared to in Unity.

However, London is not fit for parkour. Its buildings are too far apart and its streets are too wide. Without the rope launcher, which doesn’t even work right half the time, it would be impossible to traverse through usual AC means. At the same time, the rope launcher also takes away from the parkour experience. Other than that, parkour is further simplified and doesn’t have the same charm as its predecessor. Carriages give life to the city, and are nice to ride recreationally, but not very functional in chases and carriage-fights. 

I have mixed feelings about the combat. It looks amazing; the violent successive punches, cuts, stabs and revolver shots as well as the brass knuckles, cane-swords and kukri fit perfectly with the setting of Victorian London. My problem with it is there seems to be no rhythm to it. I don’t know how long it’s going to take to kill an enemy, or how many hits it takes to deal damage to an enemy. Other than that, I didn’t have a problem with the levelling system or the skill tree. Stealth is improved. The kidnapping mechanic is fun, albeit unrealistic.

My biggest gripe is how the game doesn't take itself seriously. What could be important and emotionally heavy scenes are often interrupted by bad jokes, both in the historical setting and modern-day. There’s little emotional connection between the twins and the story, the missions, or the city and that reduces the gravity of the story the game is trying to tell. We know that their father was an assassin operating in London, but all the game does with his character is use him as argument fuel between the twins, and the game completely forgot about George, whose orders the twins defy in the first place to end up in London. The game just doesn’t feel like a main AC game.

Syndicate isn’t a bad game, but is definitely the worst AC game I’ve played so far.

I completed Assassin's Creed Syndicate with 100% Synchronization, finished all the DLCs, and unlocked 54 achievements.

The biggest highlight of the game is Victorian London. Even today, The architecture, the atmosphere of the Industrial Revolution, and the incredible environmental detail make exploring the city a joy. What impressed me the most, however, was how alive London feels. NPCs are constantly working, reading newspapers, drinking coffee, playing cricket, fighting, washing clothes, or simply going about their daily lives. These little details make the world feel believable.

I also liked that they introduce two protagonists. Jacob and Evie complement each other really well, and switching between them kept the gameplay fresh. The story is decent and includes plenty of historical figures, which is something I always enjoy in an Assassin's Creed game.

Not everything worked for me, though. Many side activities became repetitive after a while. Child Liberation, Cargo Hijacks, Escort missions, and Helix Glitches weren't particularly enjoyable, while collecting every Musical Box in London was more frustrating than fun. Capturing gang territories, on the other hand, was one of my favorite activities, and I wish there had been more of it.

My biggest complaint is the parkour. It often feels clunky and unreliable. Honestly, if the rope launcher didn't exist, moving around London would have been far more frustrating.

The DLCs were all worth playing. Jack the Ripper was easily my favorite thanks to its darker atmosphere and the new Fear mechanic, which felt like a fresh addition to the series. The Last Maharaja and The Dreadful Crimes were also enjoyable and added some nice variety.

One thing that really frustrated me was the achievements. I unlocked 54, but two refused to pop. The worst was "No Ticket." I spent nearly five hours kicking enemies off trains and definitely exceeded the requirement, yet the achievement never unlocked. I'm not sure if it was a bug or a Steam synchronization issue, but it was disappointing.

Overall, Assassin's Creed Syndicate isn't my favorite Assassin's Creed game, but it's still a good one. It has some repetitive content and frustrating parkour, but the world, the Frye twins, and the Victorian setting make it well worth experiencing.

This is my favorite of the "old" AC games. And it looks and runs great on PC. Both the twins are interesting. I love London as the location. The combat can get a bit tedious (it takes many hits to bring enemies down, especially in the beginning), but the sounds and animations (like hats being flung off) are fantastic. And the soundtrack fits the world perfectly. All that being said, this is an AC game, so the world is full of collectibles and optional content. Some would say this is bloat, but it's the standard AC format (and even how the open world entries operate). I would totally recommend this game to folks wanting to try an "old" AC game that came before the "new" entries (i.e. Origins, Odyssey, and Valhalla).

As a result I dived into Syndicate pretty much completely blind after a much needed AC break of a little over a year. And I can assure you that it didn't disappoint.  
  
The exiting combat and increased fluidity of gameplay and movement is the main culprit here since previous installments felt like awkwardly moving through a jar of honey but this time around combat is fun, exiting and brutal and it made the core gameplay so much more fun than before that I wasn't even sick of it after 58 hours of gameplay.  
  
I found the story and setting far more interesting this time around as well, so much in fact that I was actually interested in sightseeing and reading Shaun's descriptions of buildings and characters.

I understand the importance of the graphical stability and the framerates and whatnot, but really, people should also talk about how fucking epic the gameplay is.

As a fan of the franchise since the first game, I don't find the story to be that good, or the characters too interesting comparing them to the first ACs. We don't need a carbon copy of Ezio, but sadly Ubisoft can't make any other set of characters as interesting as the ones in the Ezio trilogy. They aren't bad but they aren't great either

But gameplay-wise? This is where the game truly shines. I haven't experienced this kind of feeling with an AC game since I played AC2 after playing the first one.

The game takes the best bits from Unity and makes them better, like the new to the series stealth system, parkour system, customization, skills, and some resemblance to the combat (blocking at the exact time is not important tho, and the combat feels more arcade-button mashing style, way faster than any AC game)

The combat may feel clunky at first, but for me it was an acquired taste. The parkour however, feels as fluid as ever and the new grappling hook is a really nice addition in my opinion, and if you don't enjoy it you can avoid it without problem.

I also think the new missions are designed way better, I have not finished the game yet, but the missions make way more sense, are more interesting and way less repetitive than the first games. No more endless tale missions, there is an immense variety of stuff to do, and every type of mission requires a different aproach, you're not going to try the same thing inside a factory than aboard a boat.

The thing is, the stealth is implemented way better in this games than in previous ones, the mission design is more open and interesting and the navigation through the world is fluid, also taking into account the carriages.

The game is chaotic and it doesn't take itself too seriously,that is a really fresh change that the franchise needed.
For the people like me who likes the modern story, the game is a small step but in the right direction, there are just 10 minutes worth of cinematics, which kind of sucks, but it means that Ubisoft knows that the modern day storyline is necessary to keep a lot of old fans buying the games.

So, in the end, it is not the perfect AC game. it has its problems, but the gameplay is really well designed and it really shows that the developers are walking towards the right direction, in a way (if you don't b*tch a lot about every little mistake you might find just for the fuck of it) it could be said that this is the return of the franchise...

  They clearly did some research on the victorian era, and on the specific time period/decade, and you can feel it and immerse your self on it.

  The music, even though pretty simple, is probably one of my favorite OSTs on the franchise.
  Awesome sound effects.
  If you liked Assassin's Creed Odyssey and it's story, this can be your game, since the game is full of jokes and silly moments, mostly done by Jacob.
  Because of the Grappling Hook, stealth and assassinations feel really good, making you feel like some sort of mix between Assassin and Spider Man.
  Even though it's a simplified version of Assassin's Creed Unity, the parkour is still one of the best in the series, being the second best parkour system of the franchise for me.

  The game's story isn't that long, meaning you can finish it in less than 40/50H, unless you decide to go for the markers, then it can take 80 something hours.. If you are a completionist like me, and you want all the achievements, perks and 100% on everything, it took me 119H for the whole game (DLCs included), but I know it can be done in way less time.
  Compared to Unity, there aren't that many bugs. The only big bugs only happened to me after the 80H mark.
  The Dreadful Crimes DLC is probably one of the best DLCs I've ever played on any videogame in general. It is definitely a must have if you want to play this game.

Cons (-):
  The story lacks a serious tone and the villains are horribly written (with the exception of Jack the Ripper which is awesome and badass).
  The story can feel a bit random sometimes.
  Not that many memorable moments.
  Even though the Dreadful Crimes DLC is awesome, the game doesn't allow you to replay them. You will have to start a new game from scratch to replay the missions.
  Even though you have historical characters, like all Assassin's Creed games, they never felt too important, sometimes feeling really weird and wacky.
  Most of the cutscenes are a bit meh or straight up bad, specially on the Jack the Ripper DLC, where the cutscenes are literally broken.
  Voice acting could have been better, but the voices of Evie and Jacob are top tier.
  Lots of re-used animations for non-cutscene dialogues. Some feel dumb or exagerated.
  Some missions can feel a bit repetitive, but overall fun.
  Combat is trash, no questions asked. The finishers are really good though, and I suggest switching weapons from time to time.
  The perks and achievements are definitely not worth grinding or collecting, so don't lose you brain over them. If you do, I suggest you want watch/read some guides.
  It was never my thing, but there's no modern day content. There are cutscenes and a "story", but it sucks so much you might as well forget it ever happened.

Bonus stuff:
  You won't do much parkour because of the map layout, but that's part of the era the game is set in, so I can't consider this neither a pro or a con.
  Evie is waifu material.
  Jacob is comical chad.
